targetPlans.countRationale: Management-group inheritance, subscription billing/quota isolation, and resource-group lifecycle are three different Azure scope decisions. Each changes the placement outcome, while resource-specific placement observations are evidence inside those boundaries rather than additional decisions, so three retained slots are necessary and sufficient.

A deployment can independently fail because the provider namespace is unregistered, the resource type is unavailable in the chosen region, or the API version is unsupported for that type. Those three metadata checks have different evidence and remediation, which fixes the count at three.

The operating context has four material destinations: Portal for an inspected one-off change, Azure CLI for portable shell automation, Azure PowerShell for typed-object pipelines, and Bicep for declarative repeatable state. What-if is deployment validation, not a fifth tool-selection outcome.

Resource Manager creation supplies the control-plane classification, blob-content reading supplies the data-plane classification, and the management-versus-service endpoint test generalizes the boundary. These three outcomes cover plane identification without duplicating storage authorization decisions.

Safe change ownership requires one diagnosis of inherited lock effect, one preflight procedure for move support and dependent resource IDs, and one precheck/change/verify/rollback workflow. Lock-type selection and individual verification substeps live elsewhere, leaving exactly these three independent outcomes.

Activity Log caller/operation fields establish who changed control-plane state, correlationId reconstructs a multi-event change, and the Activity Log versus resource-log boundary selects the correct evidence plane. Retention export is configuration rather than another investigation decision, so the target closes with three slots.

Cloud versus external identity ownership, disable-before-delete lifecycle handling, and restoration of the original soft-deleted object answer three separate Entra administration questions. Account state and owner checks are inputs to those outcomes, not standalone learner decisions.

Assigned membership, dynamic-user membership, and dynamic-device membership require distinct population rules, while a fourth diagnosis covers privilege risk from a user-writable source attribute. Manual edits and syntax observations collapse into those mechanisms, making four the exact semantic set.

A security group must first be selected for authorization, membership must then be kept distinct from the Azure role or application permission, and nested membership must be checked against the consuming service. These three mechanisms cannot be merged without losing different access outcomes.

Group licensing needs the assignment workflow, an inventory-exhaustion diagnosis, a conflicting-service-plan diagnosis, and direct-versus-inherited source removal. The two errors have different evidence and remediation, so all four slots are material and no extra removal check is independent.

Guest invitation through review and removal is one lifecycle procedure; cross-tenant access settings govern inbound authentication, while external collaboration settings govern invitation authority and domains. Because those policy surfaces are independent, the target requires exactly three slots.

SSPR method sufficiency, per-user method registration, hybrid password writeback selection, and protected-group writeback failure each change the reset result for different reasons. Combining them would conflate policy scope, registration state, hybrid plumbing, and AD delegation, so four slots remain.

The evidence model needs sign-in stream classification, error-code/correlation tracing, the audit-log versus sign-in-log boundary, and Conditional Access result interpretation. These four log decisions isolate different identity-operation facts and replace generic filtering substeps.

Effective access is computed through inherited assignments, the union of applicable allows, matching deny assignments, the special meaning of NotActions, and assignment-condition evaluation. Each step can independently change the verdict, so the calculation needs five distinct slots.

Role design separates fitting a built-in role, creating a custom role for a stable gap, limiting custom-role assignableScopes, choosing the narrowest assignment scope, and checking DataActions for service data. Those five decisions operate on different Azure RBAC properties and cannot be reduced to one least-privilege slogan.

Azure Policy exposes materially different deny, audit, modify, and deployIfNotExists behaviors; modify also requires assignment identity permissions. Assignment/remediation/re-evaluation is a separate workflow, and exemption evidence must be distinguished from noncompliance, yielding six necessary outcomes.

CanNotDelete and ReadOnly protect different operation sets, lock inheritance determines the effective child restriction, and ScopeLocked must be separated from missing RBAC authorization. These four mechanisms fully describe lock behavior without importing data-plane examples.

Tags serve queryable ownership/classification metadata, not enforcement; resource-group tags also do not automatically propagate to children. Those are one positive classification, one control boundary, and one noninheritance diagnosis—exactly three outcomes.

Shared policy/RBAC inheritance selects a management group, separate billing/quota administration selects a subscription, and common deployment/deletion lifecycle selects a resource group. Azure exposes these three organizational boundaries, so three decisions are sufficient.

A safe Resource Manager move requires type/scope support, inclusion of provider-required dependencies, repair of references after resource IDs change, and recognition that changing region is migration or redeployment. Each produces a different stop or remediation outcome, fixing the count at four.
